Main.sentence: The International Space Station ( ISS ) is a large ___E:space station U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_station)___ that was ___E:assembled U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assembly_of_the_International_Space_Station)___ and is maintained in ___E:low Earth orbit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_Earth_orbit)___ by a collaboration of five space agencies and their contractors: ___E:NASA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA)___ (United States), ___E:Roscosmos U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roscosmos)___ (Russia), ___E:ESA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Space_Agency)___ (Europe), ___E:JAXA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JAXA)___ (Japan), and ___E:CSA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Space_Agency)___ (Canada).

As the largest space station ever constructed, it primarily serves as a platform for conducting scientific experiments in ___E:microgravity U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microgravity)___ and studying the ___E:space environment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_environment)___ .

The station is divided into two main sections: the ___E:Russian Orbital Segment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Orbital_Segment)___ (ROS), developed by Roscosmos, and the ___E:US Orbital Segment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Orbital_Segment)___ (USOS), built by NASA, ESA, JAXA, and CSA. A striking feature of the ISS is the ___E:Integrated Truss Structure U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integrated_Truss_Structure)___ , which connect the station's vast system of ___E:solar panels U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_panel)___ and ___E:radiators U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacecraft_thermal_control)___ to its pressurized modules.
These modules support diverse functions, including scientific research, crew habitation, storage, spacecraft control, and airlock operations.
The ISS has eight ___E:docking and berthing ports U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Docking_and_berthing_of_spacecraft)___ for visiting spacecraft.
The station orbits the Earth at an average altitude of 400 kilometres (250 miles)  and circles the Earth in roughly 93 minutes, completing 15.5 orbits per day.

The ___E:ISS programme U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station_programme)___ combines two previously planned crewed Earth-orbiting stations: the United States' ___E:Space Station Freedom U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Station_Freedom)___ and the Soviet Union's Mir-2 .

The ___E:first ISS module U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zarya_(ISS_module))___ was launched in 1998, with major components delivered by ___E:Proton U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proton_(rocket_family))___ and ___E:Soyuz U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_(rocket_family))___ rockets and the ___E:Space Shuttle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle)___ .

Long-term occupancy began on 2 November 2000, with the arrival of the ___E:Expedition 1 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_1)___ crew. Since then, the ISS has remained continuously inhabited for 24 years and 350 days, the longest continuous human presence in space.
As of August 2025 [update] , 290 individuals from 26 countries had visited the station.

Future plans for the ISS include the addition of at least one module, ___E:Axiom Space U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axiom_Space)___ 's ___E:Payload Power Thermal Module U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axiom_Station)___ .
The station is expected to remain operational until the end of 2030, after which it will be de-orbited using the ___E:US Deorbit Vehicle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Deorbit_Vehicle)___ .

As the ___E:space race U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_race)___ drew to a close in the early 1970s, the US and ___E:USSR U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USSR)___ began to contemplate a variety of potential collaborations in outer space.
This culminated in the 1975 ___E:Apollo-Soyuz Test Project U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo-Soyuz_Test_Project)___ , the first docking of spacecraft from two different spacefaring nations.
The ASTP was considered a success, and further joint missions were also contemplated.

One such concept was International Skylab, which proposed launching the backup ___E:Skylab B U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skylab_B)___ space station for a mission that would see multiple visits by both ___E:Apollo U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_CSM)___ and ___E:Soyuz U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_(spacecraft))___ crew vehicles.
More ambitious was the Skylab-Salyut Space Laboratory, which proposed docking the Skylab B to a Soviet ___E:Salyut U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salyut_programme)___ space station.

Falling budgets and rising ___E:Cold War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War)___ tensions in the late 1970s saw these concepts fall by the wayside, along with another plan to have the ___E:Space Shuttle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle)___ dock with a Salyut space station.
In the early 1980s, ___E:NASA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA)___ planned to launch a modular space station called Freedom as a counterpart to the Salyut and Mir space stations.

In 1984 the ESA was invited to participate in Space Station Freedom , and the ESA approved the Columbus laboratory by 1987.  The ___E:Japanese Experiment Module U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_Experiment_Module)___ (JEM), or Kibō , was announced in 1985, as part of the Freedom space station in response to a NASA request in 1982.

In early 1985, science ministers from the ___E:European Space Agency U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Space_Agency)___ (ESA) countries approved the Columbus programme, the most ambitious effort in space undertaken by that organization at the time. The plan spearheaded by Germany and Italy included a module which would be attached to Freedom , and with the capability to evolve into a full-fledged European orbital outpost before the end of the century.
Increasing costs threw these plans into doubt in the early 1990s.

Congress was unwilling to provide enough money to build and operate Freedom , and demanded NASA increase international participation to defray the rising costs or they would cancel the entire project outright.
Simultaneously, the USSR was conducting planning for the ___E:Mir-2 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mir-2)___ space station, and had begun constructing modules for the new station by the mid-1980s.

However the ___E:collapse of the Soviet Union U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collapse_of_the_Soviet_Union)___ required these plans to be greatly downscaled, and soon Mir-2 was in danger of never being launched at all.  With both space station projects in jeopardy, American and Russian officials met and proposed they be combined.

The ISS was originally intended to be a laboratory, observatory, and factory while providing transportation, maintenance, and a ___E:low Earth orbit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_Earth_orbit)___ staging base for possible future missions to the Moon, Mars, and asteroids.

However, not all of the uses envisioned in the initial ___E:memorandum of understanding U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorandum_of_understanding)___ between ___E:NASA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA)___ and ___E:Roscosmos U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roscosmos)___ have been realised.

In the ___E:2010 United States National Space Policy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_policy_of_the_Barack_Obama_administration)___ , the ISS was given additional roles of serving commercial, diplomatic,  and educational purposes.
The ISS provides a platform to conduct scientific research, with power, data, cooling, and crew available to support experiments.

Small uncrewed spacecraft can also provide platforms for experiments, especially those involving zero gravity and exposure to space, but space stations offer a long-term environment where studies can be performed potentially for decades, combined with ready access by human researchers.

The ISS simplifies individual experiments by allowing groups of experiments to share the same launches and crew time. Research is conducted in a wide variety of fields, including ___E:astrobiology U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astrobiology)___ , ___E:astronomy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomy)___ , ___E:physical sciences U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physical_science)___ , ___E:materials science U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Materials_science)___ , ___E:space weather U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_weather)___ , ___E:meteorology U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meteorology)___ , and ___E:human research U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero_g#Health_effects_of_weightlessness)___ including ___E:space medicine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_medicine)___ and the ___E:life sciences U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_science)___ .

Scientists on Earth have timely access to the data and can suggest experimental modifications to the crew. If follow-on experiments are necessary, the routinely scheduled launches of resupply craft allows new hardware to be launched with relative ease.  Crews fly ___E:expeditions U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_International_Space_Station_expeditions)___ of several months' duration, providing approximately 160 man-hours per week of labour with a crew of six. However, a considerable amount of crew time is taken up by station maintenance.

Perhaps the most notable ISS experiment is the ___E:Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpha_Magnetic_Spectrometer)___ (AMS), which is intended to detect dark matter and answer other fundamental questions about our universe.
According to NASA, the AMS is as important as the ___E:Hubble Space Telescope U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope)___ .
Currently docked on station, it could not have been easily accommodated on a free flying satellite platform because of its power and bandwidth needs.

On 3 April 2013, scientists reported that hints of ___E:dark matter U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_matter)___ may have been detected by the AMS.       According to the scientists, "The first results from the space-borne Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer confirm an unexplained excess of high-energy positrons in Earth-bound cosmic rays".

The space environment is hostile to life. Unprotected presence in space is characterised by an intense radiation field (consisting primarily of protons and other subatomic charged particles from the ___E:solar wind U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_wind)___ , in addition to ___E:cosmic rays U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_ray)___ ), high vacuum, extreme temperatures, and microgravity.

Some simple forms of life called ___E:extremophiles U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extremophile)___ ,  as well as small invertebrates called ___E:tardigrades U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tardigrade)___  can survive in this environment in an extremely dry state through ___E:desiccation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desiccation#Biology_and_ecology)___ .

Medical research improves knowledge about the effects of long-term space exposure on the human body, including ___E:muscle atrophy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muscle_atrophy)___ , ___E:bone loss U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osteoporosis)___ , and fluid shift.

These data will be used to determine whether high duration ___E:human spaceflight U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_spaceflight)___ and ___E:space colonisation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_colonisation)___ are feasible.

In 2006, data on bone loss and muscular atrophy suggested that there would be a significant risk of fractures and movement problems if astronauts landed on a planet after a lengthy interplanetary cruise, such as the six-month interval required to ___E:travel to Mars U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_mission_to_Mars)___ .

Medical studies are conducted aboard the ISS on behalf of the ___E:National Space Biomedical Research Institute U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Space_Biomedical_Research_Institute)___ (NSBRI).

Prominent among these is the ___E:Advanced Diagnostic Ultrasound in Microgravity U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advanced_Diagnostic_Ultrasound_in_Microgravity)___ study in which astronauts perform ultrasound scans under the guidance of remote experts.
The study considers the diagnosis and treatment of medical conditions in space.
Usually, there is no physician on board the ISS and diagnosis of medical conditions is a challenge.
It is anticipated that remotely guided ultrasound scans will have application on Earth in emergency and rural care situations where access to a trained physician is difficult.

In August 2020, scientists reported that ___E:bacteria U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bacteria)___ from Earth, particularly Deinococcus radiodurans bacteria, which is highly resistant to ___E:environmental hazards U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_hazard)___ , were found to survive for three years in ___E:outer space U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outer_space)___ , based on studies conducted on the International Space Station.

These findings supported the notion of ___E:panspermia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panspermia)___ , the hypothesis that ___E:life U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life)___ exists throughout the ___E:Universe U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universe)___ , distributed in various ways, including ___E:space dust U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_dust)___ , ___E:meteoroids U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meteoroid)___ , ___E:asteroids U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asteroid)___ , ___E:comets U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comet)___ , ___E:planetoids U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minor_planet)___ or ___E:contaminated U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contamination)___ ___E:spacecraft U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacecraft)___ .

___E:Remote sensing U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remote_sensing)___ of the Earth, astronomy, and deep space research on the ISS have significantly increased during the 2010s after the completion of the ___E:US Orbital Segment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Orbital_Segment)___ in 2011. Throughout the more than 20 years of the ISS program, researchers aboard the ISS and on the ground have examined ___E:aerosols U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerosol)___ , ___E:ozone U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozone)___ , ___E:lightning U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lightning)___ , and ___E:oxides U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxide)___ in Earth's atmosphere, as well as the ___E:Sun U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun)___ , cosmic rays, ___E:cosmic dust U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_dust)___ , ___E:antimatter U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antimatter)___ , and dark matter in the universe.

Examples of Earth-viewing remote sensing experiments that have flown on the ISS are the ___E:Orbiting Carbon Observatory 3 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbiting_Carbon_Observatory_3)___ , ___E:ISS-RapidScat U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISS-RapidScat)___ , ___E:ECOSTRESS U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECOSTRESS)___ , the ___E:Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Ecosystem_Dynamics_Investigation)___ , and the ___E:Cloud Aerosol Transport System U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloud_Aerosol_Transport_System)___ .

ISS-based astronomy telescopes and experiments include ___E:SOLAR U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SOLAR_(ISS))___ , the ___E:Neutron Star Interior Composition Explorer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron_Star_Interior_Composition_Explorer)___ , the ___E:Calorimetric Electron Telescope U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calorimetric_Electron_Telescope)___ , the ___E:Monitor of All-sky X-ray Image (MAXI) U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MAXI_(ISS_experiment))___ , and the ___E:Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpha_Magnetic_Spectrometer)___ .
Researchers are investigating the effect of the station's near-weightless environment on the evolution, development, growth and internal processes of plants and animals.

In response to some of the data, NASA wants to investigate ___E:microgravity U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microgravity)___ 's effects on the growth of three-dimensional, human-like tissues and the unusual ___E:protein crystals U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protein_crystal)___ that can be formed in space.
Investigating the physics of fluids in microgravity will provide better models of the behaviour of fluids.
Because fluids can be almost completely combined in microgravity, physicists investigate fluids that do not mix well on Earth.
Examining reactions that are slowed by low gravity and low temperatures will improve our understanding of ___E:superconductivity U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superconductivity)___ .

The study of ___E:materials science U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Materials_science)___ is an important ISS research activity, with the objective of reaping economic benefits through the improvement of techniques used on Earth.
Other areas of interest include the effect of low gravity on combustion, through the study of the efficiency of burning and control of emissions and pollutants.
These findings may improve knowledge about energy production and lead to economic and environmental benefits.

The ISS provides a location in the relative safety of low Earth orbit to test spacecraft systems that will be required for long-duration missions to the Moon and Mars. This provides experience in operations, maintenance, and repair and replacement activities on-orbit.
This will help develop essential skills in operating spacecraft farther from Earth, reduce mission risks, and advance the capabilities of interplanetary spacecraft.

Referring to the ___E:MARS-500 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MARS-500)___ experiment, a crew isolation experiment conducted on Earth, ESA states, "Whereas the ISS is essential for answering questions concerning the possible impact of weightlessness, radiation and other space-specific factors, aspects such as the effect of long-term isolation and confinement can be more appropriately addressed via ground-based simulations".
Sergey Krasnov, the head of human space flight programmes for Russia's space agency, Roscosmos, in 2011 suggested a "shorter version" of MARS-500 may be carried out on the ISS.

In 2009, noting the value of the partnership framework itself, Sergey Krasnov wrote, "When compared with partners acting separately, partners developing complementary abilities and resources could give us much more assurance of the success and safety of space exploration.

The ISS is helping further advance near-Earth space exploration and realisation of prospective programmes of research and exploration of the Solar system, including the Moon and Mars."  ___E:A crewed mission to Mars U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_mission_to_Mars)___ may be a multinational effort involving space agencies and countries outside the current ISS partnership.
In 2010, ESA Director-General Jean-Jacques Dordain stated his agency was ready to propose to the other four partners that China, India, and South Korea be invited to join the ISS partnership.

NASA chief ___E:Charles Bolden U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Bolden)___ stated in February 2011, "Any mission to Mars is likely to be a global effort."  Currently, ___E:US federal legislation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolf_Amendment)___ prevents NASA co-operation with China on space projects without approval by the ___E:FBI U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FBI)___ and Congress.

The ISS crew provides opportunities for students on Earth by running student-developed experiments, making educational demonstrations, allowing for student participation in classroom versions of ISS experiments, and directly engaging students using radio, and email.
ESA offers a wide range of free teaching materials that can be downloaded for use in classrooms.
In one lesson, students can navigate a ___E:3D model U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3D_modeling)___ of the interior and exterior of the ISS, and face spontaneous challenges to solve in real time.

The ___E:Japanese Aerospace Exploration Agency U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_Aerospace_Exploration_Agency)___ (JAXA) aims to inspire children to "pursue craftsmanship" and to heighten their "awareness of the importance of life and their responsibilities in society".

Through a series of education guides, students develop a deeper understanding of the past and near-term future of crewed space flight, as well as that of Earth and life.   In the JAXA "Seeds in Space" experiments, the mutation effects of spaceflight on plant seeds aboard the ISS are explored by growing sunflower seeds that have flown on the ISS for about nine months.
In the first phase of Kibō utilisation from 2008 to mid-2010, researchers from more than a dozen Japanese universities conducted experiments in diverse fields.
Cultural activities are another major objective of the ISS programme.
Tetsuo Tanaka, the director of JAXA's Space Environment and Utilization Center, has said: "There is something about space that touches even people who are not interested in science."

___E:Amateur Radio on the ISS U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amateur_Radio_on_the_International_Space_Station)___ (ARISS) is a volunteer programme that encourages students worldwide to pursue careers in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics, through ___E:amateur radio U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amateur_radio)___ communications opportunities with the ISS crew. ARISS is an international working group, consisting of delegations from nine countries including several in Europe, as well as Japan, Russia, Canada, and the United States.

In areas where radio equipment cannot be used, ___E:speakerphones U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speakerphone)___ connect students to ground stations which then connect the calls to the space station.
First Orbit is a 2011 feature-length documentary film about ___E:Vostok 1 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vostok_1)___ , the first crewed space flight around the Earth.

By matching the orbit of the ISS to that of Vostok 1 as closely as possible, in terms of ground path and time of day, documentary filmmaker ___E:Christopher Riley U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Riley)___ and ESA astronaut ___E:Paolo Nespoli U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paolo_Nespoli)___ were able to film the view that ___E:Yuri Gagarin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuri_Gagarin)___ saw on his pioneering orbital space flight.
This new footage was cut together with the original Vostok 1 mission audio recordings sourced from the Russian State Archive.

Nespoli is credited as the ___E:director of photography U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinematographer)___ for this documentary film, as he recorded the majority of the footage himself during ___E:Expedition 26 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_26)___ / ___E:27 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_27)___ .
The film was streamed in a global YouTube premiere in 2011 under a free licence through the website firstorbit.org .

In May 2013, commander ___E:Chris Hadfield U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Hadfield)___ shot a music video of ___E:David Bowie U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Bowie)___ 's " ___E:Space Oddity U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Oddity)___ " on board the station, which was released on YouTube.
It was the first music video filmed in space.

In November 2017, while participating in ___E:Expedition 52 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_52)___ / ___E:53 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_53)___ on the ISS, ___E:Paolo Nespoli U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paolo_Nespoli)___ made two recordings of his spoken voice (one in English and the other in his native Italian), for use on ___E:Wikipedia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia)___ articles.
These were the first content made in space specifically for Wikipedia.
In November 2021, a ___E:virtual reality U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtual_reality)___ exhibit called The Infinite featuring life aboard the ISS was announced.
Involving five space programs and fifteen countries,  the International Space Station is the most politically and legally complex space exploration programme in history.
The 1998 Space Station Intergovernmental Agreement sets forth the primary framework for international cooperation among the parties.
A series of subsequent agreements govern other aspects of the station, ranging from jurisdictional issues to a code of conduct among visiting astronauts.
Brazil was also invited to participate in the programme, the only developing country to receive such an invitation.
Under the agreement framework, Brazil was to provide six pieces of hardware, and in exchange, would receive ISS utilization rights.
However, Brazil was unable to deliver any of the elements due to a lack of funding and political priority within the country.
Brazil officially dropped out of the ISS programme in 2007.

Following the ___E:2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine)___ , continued cooperation between Russia and other countries on the International Space Station has been put into question.

Roscosmos Director General ___E:Dmitry Rogozin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dmitry_Rogozin)___ insinuated that Russian withdrawal could cause the International Space Station to de-orbit due to lack of reboost capabilities, writing in a series of tweets, "If you block cooperation with us, who will save the ISS from an unguided de-orbit to impact on the territory of the US or Europe?
There's also the chance of impact of the 500-ton construction in India or China.
Do you want to threaten them with such a prospect?
The ISS doesn't fly over Russia, so all the risk is yours.

Are you ready for it?"  (This latter claim is untrue: the ISS flies over all parts of the Earth between 51.6 degrees latitude north and south, approximately the latitude of ___E:Saratov U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saratov)___ .) Rogozin later tweeted that normal relations between ISS partners could only be restored once sanctions have been lifted, and indicated that Roscosmos would submit proposals to the Russian government on ending cooperation.
NASA stated that, if necessary, US corporation ___E:Northrop Grumman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northrop_Grumman)___ has offered a reboost capability that would keep the ISS in orbit.

On 26 July 2022, ___E:Yury Borisov U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yury_Borisov)___ , Rogozin's successor as head of Roscosmos, submitted to Russian President Putin plans for withdrawal from the programme after 2024.  However, Robyn Gatens, the NASA official in charge of the space station, responded that NASA had not received any formal notices from Roscosmos concerning withdrawal plans.
The International Space Station is a product of global collaboration, with its components manufactured across the world.

The modules of the ___E:Russian Orbital Segment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Orbital_Segment)___ , including Zarya and Zvezda , were produced at the ___E:Khrunichev State Research and Production Space Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khrunichev_State_Research_and_Production_Space_Center)___ in Moscow.
Zvezda was initially manufactured in 1985 as a component for the Mir-2 space station, which was never launched.

Much of the ___E:US Orbital Segment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Orbital_Segment)___ , including the Destiny and Unity modules, the ___E:Integrated Truss Structure U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integrated_Truss_Structure)___ , and ___E:solar arrays U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrical_system_of_the_International_Space_Station)___ , were built at NASA's ___E:Marshall Space Flight Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshall_Space_Flight_Center)___ in ___E:Huntsville, Alabama U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huntsville,_Alabama)___ and ___E:Michoud Assembly Facility U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michoud_Assembly_Facility)___ in ___E:New Orleans U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans)___ .

These components underwent final assembly and processing for launch at the ___E:Operations and Checkout Building U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operations_and_Checkout_Building)___ and the ___E:Space Station Processing Facility U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Station_Processing_Facility)___ (SSPF) at the ___E:Kennedy Space Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center)___ in Florida.

The US Orbital Segment also hosts the ___E:Columbus U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_(ISS_module))___ module contributed by the ___E:European Space Agency U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Space_Agency)___ and built in Germany, the ___E:Kibō U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kib%C5%8D_(ISS_module))___ module contributed by ___E:Japan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JAXA)___ and built at the ___E:Tsukuba Space Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsukuba_Space_Center)___ and the ___E:Institute of Space and Astronautical Science U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_of_Space_and_Astronautical_Science)___ , along with the ___E:Canadarm2 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadarm2)___ and ___E:Dextre U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dextre)___ , a joint Canadian-U.S. endeavor.
All of these components were shipped to the SSPF for launch processing.
The assembly of the International Space Station, a major endeavour in ___E:space architecture U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_architecture)___ , began in November 1998.
Modules in the Russian segment launched and docked autonomously, with the exception of Rassvet .

Other modules and components were delivered by the ___E:Space Shuttle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle)___ , which then had to be installed by astronauts either remotely using robotic arms or during spacewalks, more formally known as ___E:extra-vehicular activities U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extravehicular_activity)___ (EVAs).
By 5 June 2011 astronauts had made over 159 EVAs to add components to the station, totaling more than 1,000 hours in space.

The beginning of the core of the ISS's tenure in orbit was the launch of the Russian-built Zarya module atop a ___E:Proton rocket U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proton_(rocket_family))___ on 20 November 1998. Zarya provided propulsion, ___E:attitude control U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacecraft_attitude_control)___ , communications, and electrical power.

Two weeks later on 4 December 1998, the American-made Unity was ferried aboard ___E:Space Shuttle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle)___ ___E:Endeavour U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Endeavour)___ on ___E:STS-88 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-88)___ and joined with Zarya .
Unity provided the connection between the Russian and US segments of the station and would provide ports to connect future modules and visiting spacecraft.

While the connection of two modules built on different continents, by nations that were once bitter rivals was a significant milestone, these two initial modules lacked life-support systems and the ISS remained unmanned for the next two years.
At the time, the Russian station Mir was still inhabited.
The turning point arrived in July 2000 with the launch of the Zvezda module.
Equipped with living quarters and life-support systems, Zvezda enabled continuous human presence aboard the station.
The first crew, ___E:Expedition 1 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_1)___ , arrived that November aboard ___E:Soyuz TM-31 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_TM-31)___ .
The ISS grew steadily over the following years, with modules delivered by both Russian rockets and the Space Shuttle.
Expedition 1 arrived midway between the Space Shuttle flights of missions ___E:STS-92 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-92)___ and ___E:STS-97 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-97)___ .

These two flights each added segments of the station's ___E:Integrated Truss Structure U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integrated_Truss_Structure)___ , which provided the station with ___E:Ku band U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ku_band)___ communications, additional attitude control needed for the additional mass of the USOS, and additional solar arrays.
Over the next two years, the station continued to expand.
A ___E:Soyuz-U U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz-U)___ rocket delivered the ___E:Pirs docking compartment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pirs_(ISS_module))___ .

The Space Shuttles Discovery , Atlantis , and Endeavour delivered the American Destiny laboratory and ___E:Quest airlock U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quest_Joint_Airlock)___ , in addition to the station's main robot arm, the ___E:Canadarm2 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadarm2)___ , and several more segments of the Integrated Truss Structure.

Tragedy struck in 2003 with the ___E:loss of the Space Shuttle Columbia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster)___ , which grounded the rest of the Shuttle fleet, halting construction of the ISS.
Assembly resumed in 2006 with the arrival of ___E:STS-115 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-115)___ with Atlantis , which delivered the station's second set of solar arrays.

Several more truss segments and a third set of arrays were delivered on ___E:STS-116 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-116)___ , ___E:STS-117 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-117)___ , and ___E:STS-118 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-118)___ .
As a result of the major expansion of the station's power-generating capabilities, more modules could be accommodated, and the US Harmony module and Columbus European laboratory were added.
These were soon followed by the first two components of the Japanese Kibō laboratory.
In March 2009, ___E:STS-119 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-119)___ completed the Integrated Truss Structure with the installation of the fourth and final set of solar arrays.
The final section of Kibō was delivered in July 2009 on ___E:STS-127 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-127)___ , followed by the Russian Poisk module.

The US Tranquility module was delivered in February 2010 during ___E:STS-130 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-130)___ , alongside the Cupola , followed by the penultimate Russian module, Rassvet , in May 2010. Rassvet was delivered by Space Shuttle Atlantis on ___E:STS-132 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-132)___ in exchange for the Russian Proton delivery of the US-funded Zarya module in 1998.  The last pressurised module of the USOS, Leonardo , was brought to the station in February 2011 on the final flight of Discovery , ___E:STS-133 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-133)___ .
Russia's new primary research module Nauka docked in July 2021,  along with the European Robotic Arm which can relocate itself to different parts of the Russian modules of the station.
Russia's latest addition, the ___E:Prichal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prichal_(ISS_module))___ module, docked in November 2021.
As of June 2025, nasa.gov states that there are 43 different modules and elements installed on the ISS.
The ISS functions as a modular space station, enabling the addition or removal of modules from its structure for increased adaptability.

Zarya ( ___E:Russian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_language)___ : Заря , lit. 'Sunrise' [c] ), also known as the Functional Cargo Block (Russian: Функционально-грузовой блок ), was the inaugural component of the ISS. Launched in 1998, it initially served as the ISS's power source, storage, propulsion, and guidance system.
As the station has grown, Zarya' s role has transitioned primarily to storage, both internally and in its external fuel tanks.

A descendant of the ___E:TKS spacecraft U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TKS_(spacecraft))___ used in the ___E:Salyut programme U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salyut_programme)___ , Zarya was built in Russia but is owned by the United States.
Its name symbolizes the beginning of a new era of international space cooperation.

Unity , also known as Node 1 , is the inaugural U.S.-built component of the ISS.   Serving as the connection between the Russian and U.S. segments, this cylindrical module features six ___E:Common Berthing Mechanism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_Berthing_Mechanism)___ locations ( ___E:forward U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forward_(aircraft))___ , ___E:aft U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aft)___ , ___E:port U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_(nautical))___ , ___E:starboard U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starboard)___ , ___E:zenith U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zenith)___ , and ___E:nadir U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadir)___ ) for attaching additional modules.

Measuring 4.57 metres (15.0 ft) in diameter and 5.47 metres (17.9 ft) in length, Unity was constructed of steel by ___E:Boeing U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing)___ for NASA at the ___E:Marshall Space Flight Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshall_Space_Flight_Center)___ in ___E:Huntsville, Alabama U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huntsville,_Alabama)___ .
It was the first of three connecting nodes – Unity , Harmony , and Tranquility – that forms the structural backbone of the U.S. segment of the ISS.

Zvezda (Russian: Звезда , lit. 'star') launched in July 2000, is the core of the ___E:Russian Orbital Segment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Orbital_Segment)___ of the ISS. Initially providing essential living quarters and ___E:life-support systems U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life-support_system)___ , it enabled the first continuous human presence aboard the station.
While additional modules have expanded the ISS's capabilities, Zvezda remains the command and control center for the Russian segment and it is where crews gather during emergencies.

A descendant of the Salyut programme's DOS spacecraft, Zvezda was built by ___E:RKK Energia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RKK_Energia)___ and launched atop a ___E:Proton rocket U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proton_(rocket_family))___ .

The Destiny laboratory is the primary research facility for U.S. experiments on the ISS. NASA's first permanent orbital research station since Skylab, the module was built by Boeing and launched aboard Space Shuttle ___E:Atlantis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis)___ during ___E:STS-98 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-98)___ .
Attached to Unity over a period of five days in February 2001, Destiny has been a hub for scientific research ever since.
Within Destiny , astronauts conduct experiments in fields such as medicine, engineering, biotechnology, physics, materials science, and Earth science.
Researchers worldwide benefit from these studies.
The module also houses life-support systems, including the ___E:Oxygen Generating System U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen_Generating_System)___ .

The Quest Joint Airlock enables ___E:extravehicular activities U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extravehicular_activity)___ (EVAs) using either the U.S. ___E:Extravehicular Mobility Unit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extravehicular_Mobility_Unit)___ (EMU) or the Russian ___E:Orlan space suit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orlan_space_suit)___ .
Before its installation, conducting EVAs from the ISS was challenging due to a variety of system and design differences.

Only the Orlan suit could be used from the Transfer Chamber on the Zvezda module (which was not a purpose-built airlock) and the EMU could only be used from the airlock on a visiting Space Shuttle, which could not accommodate the Orlan.

Launched aboard Space Shuttle ___E:Atlantis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis)___ during ___E:STS-104 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-104)___ in July 2001 and attached to the Unity module, Quest is a 6.1-metre-long (20 ft), 4.0-metre-wide (13 ft) structure built by Boeing.

It houses the crew airlock for astronaut egress, an equipment airlock for suit storage, and has facilities to accommodate astronauts during their overnight pre-breathe procedures to prevent decompression sickness.

The crew airlock, derived from the Space Shuttle, features essential equipment like lighting, handrails, and an Umbilical Interface Assembly (UIA) that provides life-support and communication systems for up to two spacesuits simultaneously.
These can be either two EMUs, two Orlan suits, or one of each design.

Poisk (Russian: По́иск , lit. 'Search'), also known as the Mini-Research Module 2 (Russian: Малый исследовательский модуль 2 ), serves as both a secondary airlock on the Russian segment of the ISS and supports docking for Soyuz and Progress spacecraft, facilitates propellant transfers from the latter.

Launched on 10 November 2009 attached to a modified ___E:Progress spacecraft U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progress_spacecraft)___ , called ___E:Progress M-MIM2 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progress_M-MIM2)___ .

Poisk provides facilities to maintain Orlan spacesuits and is equipped with two inward-opening hatches, a design change from Mir , which encountered a dangerous situation caused by an outward-opening hatch that opened too quickly because of a small amount of air pressure remaining in the airlock.
Since the departure of ___E:Pirs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pirs_(ISS_module))___ in 2021, it's become the sole airlock on the Russian segment.
Harmony , or Node 2 , is the central connecting hub of the US segment of the ISS, linking the U.S., European, and Japanese laboratory modules.
It's also been called the "utility hub" of the ISS as it provides essential power, data, and life-support systems.
The module also houses sleeping quarters for four crew members.

Launched on 23 October 2007 aboard Space Shuttle ___E:Discovery U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery)___ on ___E:STS-120 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-120)___ ,   Harmony was initially attached to the Unity   before being relocated to its permanent position at the front of the Destiny laboratory on 14 November 2007.  This expansion added significant living space to the ISS, marking a key milestone in the construction of the U.S. segment.

Tranquility , also known as Node 3 , is a module of the ISS. It contains environmental control systems, ___E:life-support systems U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life-support_system)___ , a toilet, exercise equipment, and an observation ___E:cupola U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cupola_(ISS_module))___ .

The European Space Agency and the ___E:Italian Space Agency U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_Space_Agency)___ had Tranquility manufactured by ___E:Thales Alenia Space U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thales_Alenia_Space)___ .

A ceremony on 20 November 2009 transferred ownership of the module to NASA.  On 8 February 2010, NASA launched the module on the Space Shuttle's ___E:STS-130 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-130)___ mission.
Columbus is a science laboratory that is part of the ISS and is the largest single contribution to the station made by the European Space Agency.

Like the Harmony and Tranquility modules, the Columbus laboratory was constructed in ___E:Turin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turin)___ , Italy by ___E:Thales Alenia Space U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thales_Alenia_Space)___ .
The functional equipment and software of the lab was designed by ___E:EADS U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EADS)___ in ___E:Bremen U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bremen)___ , Germany.

It was also integrated in Bremen before being flown to the Kennedy Space Center in Florida in an ___E:Airbus Beluga U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airbus_Beluga)___ jet. It was launched aboard Space Shuttle Atlantis on 7 February 2008, on flight ___E:STS-122 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-122)___ .
It is designed for ten years of operation.

The module is controlled by the ___E:Columbus Control Centre U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Control_Centre)___ , located at the ___E:German Space Operations Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Space_Operations_Center)___ , part of the ___E:German Aerospace Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Aerospace_Center)___ in ___E:Oberpfaffenhofen U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oberpfaffenhofen)___ near ___E:Munich U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich)___ , Germany.

The European Space Agency has spent ___E:€ U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euro)___ 1.4 billion (about ___E:US$ U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_dollar)___ 1.6 billion) on building Columbus , including the experiments it carries and the ground control infrastructure necessary to operate them.

Kibō (Japanese: きぼう; lit. 'hope') , also known as the Japanese Experiment Module , is Japan's research facility on the ISS. It is the largest single module on the ISS, consisting of a pressurized lab, an exposed facility for conducting experiments in the space environment, two storage compartments, and a robotic arm. Attached to the Harmony module, Kibō was assembled in space over three Space Shuttle missions: ___E:STS-123 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-123)___ , ___E:STS-124 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-124)___ and ___E:STS-127 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-127)___ .

The Cupola is an ___E:ESA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESA)___ -built observatory module of the ISS. Its name derives from the Italian word cupola , which means " ___E:dome U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dome)___ ".
Its seven windows are used to conduct experiments, dockings and observations of Earth.
It was launched aboard Space Shuttle mission STS-130 on 8 February 2010 and attached to the Tranquility (Node 3) module.
With the Cupola attached, ISS assembly reached 85 per cent completion.
The Cupola 's central window has a diameter of 80 cm (31 in).

Rassvet (Russian: Рассвет , lit. 'first light'), also known as the Mini-Research Module 1 (Russian: Малый исследовательский модуль 1 ) and formerly known as the Docking Cargo Module is primarily used for cargo storage and as a docking port for visiting spacecraft on the Russian segment of the ISS. Rassvet replaced the cancelled Docking and Storage Module and used a design largely based on the Mir Docking Module built in 1995.

Rassvet was delivered in on 14 May 2010 Space Shuttle ___E:Atlantis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis)___ on ___E:STS-132 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-132)___ in exchange for the Russian Proton delivery of the US-funded Zarya module in 1998.  Rassvet was attached to Zarya shortly thereafter.

The Leonardo Permanent Multipurpose Module (PMM) was flown into space aboard the Space Shuttle Discovery on ___E:STS-133 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-133)___ on 24 February 2011 and installed on 1 March.
Leonardo is primarily used for storage of spares, supplies and waste on the ISS, which was until then stored in many different places within the space station.
It is also the personal hygiene area for the astronauts who live in the ___E:US Orbital Segment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Orbital_Segment)___ .
The Leonardo PMM was a ___E:Multi-Purpose Logistics Module U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-Purpose_Logistics_Module)___ (MPLM) before 2011, but was modified into its current configuration.
It was formerly one of two MPLM used for bringing cargo to and from the ISS with the Space Shuttle.
The module was named for Italian polymath ___E:Leonardo da Vinci U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonardo_da_Vinci)___ .

The ___E:Bigelow Expandable Activity Module U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bigelow_Expandable_Activity_Module)___ (BEAM) is an experimental ___E:expandable U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inflatable_space_habitat)___ ___E:space station module U:(https://en.wikipedia.org#Pressurised_modules)___ developed by ___E:Bigelow Aerospace U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bigelow_Aerospace)___ , under contract to NASA, for testing as a temporary module on the International Space Station (ISS) from 2016 to at least 2020. It arrived at the ISS on 10 April 2016,  was berthed to the station on 16 April at Tranquility Node 3, and was expanded and pressurized on 28 May 2016. In December 2021, Bigelow Aerospace conveyed ownership of the module to NASA, as a result of Bigelow's cessation of activity.

The ___E:International Docking Adapter U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Docking_Adapter)___ (IDA) is a ___E:spacecraft docking system adapter U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Docking_and_berthing_of_spacecraft#Adapters)___ developed to convert ___E:APAS-95 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/APAS-95)___ to the ___E:NASA Docking System U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_Docking_System)___ (NDS).

An IDA is placed on each of the ISS's two open ___E:Pressurized Mating Adapters U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pressurized_Mating_Adapters)___ (PMAs), both of which are connected to the Harmony module.
Two International Docking Adapters are currently installed aboard the Station.

Originally, ___E:IDA-1 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Docking_Adapter)___ was planned to be installed on PMA-2, located at Harmony 's forward port, and ___E:IDA-2 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Docking_Adapter#IDA-2)___ would be installed on PMA-3 at Harmony 's zenith.

After IDA 1 was destroyed in ___E:a launch incident U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpaceX_CRS-7)___ , ___E:IDA-2 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Docking_Adapter#IDA-2)___ was installed on PMA-2 on 19 August 2016,  while ___E:IDA-3 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Docking_Adapter#IDA-3)___ was later installed on PMA-3 on 21 August 2019.

The NanoRacks Bishop Airlock Module is a ___E:commercially U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_use_of_space)___ funded ___E:airlock U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airlock)___ module launched to the ISS on ___E:SpaceX CRS-21 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpaceX_CRS-21)___ on 6 December 2020.   The module was built by ___E:NanoRacks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NanoRacks)___ , ___E:Thales Alenia Space U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thales_Alenia_Space)___ , and Boeing.

It will be used to deploy ___E:CubeSats U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CubeSat)___ , ___E:small satellites U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Small_satellite)___ , and other external payloads for NASA, ___E:CASIS U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CASIS)___ , and other commercial and governmental customers.

Nauka (Russian: Наука , lit. 'Science'), also known as the Multipurpose Laboratory Module, Upgrade (Russian: Многоцелевой лабораторный модуль, усоверше́нствованный ), is a Roscosmos-funded component of the ISS that was launched on 21 July 2021, 14:58 UTC. In the original ISS plans, Nauka was to use the location of the ___E:Docking and Stowage Module U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rassvet_(ISS_module)#Initial_planning)___ (DSM), but the DSM was later replaced by the Rassvet module and moved to Zarya ' s nadir port. Nauka was successfully docked to Zvezda ' s nadir port on 29 July 2021, 13:29 UTC, replacing the Pirs module.
It had a temporary docking adapter on its nadir port for crewed and uncrewed missions until Prichal arrival, where just before its arrival it was removed by a departing Progress spacecraft.

Prichal (Russian: Причал , lit. 'pier') is a 4-tonne (8,800 lb) spherical module that serves as a docking hub for the Russian segment of the ISS. Launched in November 2021, Prichal provides additional docking ports for Soyuz and Progress spacecraft, as well as potential future modules.
Prichal features six docking ports: forward, aft, port, starboard, zenith, and nadir.
One of these ports, equipped with an active hybrid docking system, enabled it to dock with the Nauka module.
The remaining five ports are passive hybrids, allowing for docking of Soyuz, Progress, and heavier modules, as well as future spacecraft with modified docking systems.
As of 2024, the forward, aft, port and starboard docking ports remain covered.

Prichal was initially intended to be an element of the now canceled ___E:Orbital Piloted Assembly and Experiment Complex U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_Piloted_Assembly_and_Experiment_Complex)___ .
The ISS has a large number of external components that do not require pressurisation.

The largest of these is the ___E:Integrated Truss Structure U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integrated_Truss_Structure)___ (ITS), to which the station's main ___E:solar arrays U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photovoltaic_system)___ and ___E:thermal radiators U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/External_Active_Thermal_Control_System)___ are mounted.
The ITS consists of ten separate segments forming a structure 108.5 metres (356 ft) long.

The station was intended to have several smaller external components, such as six robotic arms, three ___E:External Stowage Platforms U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/External_Stowage_Platform)___ (ESPs) and four ___E:ExPRESS Logistics Carriers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ExPRESS_Logistics_Carrier)___ (ELCs).

While these platforms allow experiments (including ___E:MISSE U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Materials_International_Space_Station_Experiment)___ , the STP-H3 and the ___E:Robotic Refueling Mission U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robotic_Refueling_Mission)___ ) to be deployed and conducted in the vacuum of space by providing electricity and processing experimental data locally, their primary function is to store spare ___E:Orbital Replacement Units U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_replacement_unit)___ (ORUs).
ORUs are parts that can be replaced when they fail or pass their design life, including pumps, storage tanks, antennas, and battery units.

Such units are replaced either by astronauts during EVA or by robotic arms.  Several shuttle missions were dedicated to the delivery of ORUs, including ___E:STS-129 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-129)___ ,  STS-133  and STS-134.  As of January 2011 [update] , only one other mode of transportation of ORUs had been used – the Japanese cargo vessel ___E:HTV-2 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H-II_Transfer_Vehicle)___ – which delivered an FHRC and CTC-2 via its Exposed Pallet (EP).  [needs update]

There are also smaller exposure facilities mounted directly to laboratory modules; the Kibō ___E:Exposed Facility U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kibo_(ISS_module))___ serves as an external " ___E:porch U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porch)___ " for the Kibō complex,  and a facility on the European Columbus laboratory provides power and data connections for experiments such as the ___E:European Technology Exposure Facility U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Technology_Exposure_Facility)___   and the ___E:Atomic Clock Ensemble in Space U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_Clock_Ensemble_in_Space)___ .

A ___E:remote sensing U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remote_sensing)___ instrument, ___E:SAGE III-ISS U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SAGE_III_on_ISS)___ , was delivered to the station in February 2017 aboard ___E:CRS-10 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpaceX_CRS-10)___ ,  and the ___E:NICER U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron_Star_Interior_Composition_Explorer)___ experiment was delivered aboard ___E:CRS-11 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpaceX_CRS-11)___ in June 2017.  The largest scientific payload externally mounted to the ISS is the ___E:Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpha_Magnetic_Spectrometer)___ (AMS), a particle physics experiment launched on STS-134 in May 2011, and mounted externally on the ITS. The AMS measures cosmic rays to look for evidence of dark matter and antimatter.

The commercial Bartolomeo External Payload Hosting Platform, manufactured by Airbus, was launched on 6 March 2020 aboard ___E:CRS-20 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpaceX_CRS-20)___ and attached to the European Columbus module.

It will provide an additional 12 external payload slots, supplementing the eight on the ___E:ExPRESS Logistics Carriers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ExPRESS_Logistics_Carrier)___ , ten on Kibō , and four on Columbus .
The system is designed to be robotically serviced and will require no astronaut intervention.
It is named after Christopher Columbus's younger brother.
In May 2010, equipment for Nauka was launched on STS-132 (as part of an agreement with NASA) and delivered by Space Shuttle Atlantis .
Weighing 1.4 metric tons, the equipment was attached to the outside of Rassvet (MRM-1).

It included a spare elbow joint for the ___E:European Robotic Arm U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Robotic_Arm)___ (ERA) (which was launched with Nauka ) and an ERA-portable workpost used during EVAs, as well as RTOd add-on heat radiator and internal hardware alongside the pressurized experiment airlock.
The RTOd radiator adds additional cooling capability to Nauka , which enables the module to host more scientific experiments.
The ERA was used to remove the RTOd radiator from Rassvet and transferred over to Nauka during VKD-56 spacewalk.
Later it was activated and fully deployed on VKD-58 spacewalk.
This process took several months.

A portable work platform was also transferred over in August 2023 during VKD-60 spacewalk, which can attach to the end of the ERA to allow cosmonauts to "ride" on the end of the arm during spacewalks.

However, even after several months of outfitting EVAs and RTOd heat radiator installation, six months later, the RTOd radiator malfunctioned before active use of Nauka (the purpose of RTOd installation is to radiate heat from Nauka experiments).
The malfunction, a leak, rendered the RTOd radiator unusable for Nauka.
This is the third ISS radiator leak after ___E:Soyuz MS-22 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_MS-22)___ and ___E:Progress MS-21 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progress_MS-21)___ radiator leaks.
If a spare RTOd is not available, Nauka experiments will have to rely on Nauka's main launch radiator and the module could never be used to its full capacity.
Another MLM outfitting is a 4 segment external payload interface called means of attachment of large payloads (Sredstva Krepleniya Krupnogabaritnykh Obyektov, SKKO).

Delivered in two parts to Nauka by ___E:Progress MS-18 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progress_MS-18)___ (LCCS part) and ___E:Progress MS-21 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progress_MS-21)___ (SCCCS part) as part of the module activation outfitting process.
It was taken outside and installed on the ERA aft facing base point on Nauka during the VKD-55 spacewalk.

The Integrated Truss Structure (ITS) serves as a base for the station's primary remote manipulator system, the ___E:Mobile Servicing System U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobile_Servicing_System)___ (MSS), which is composed of three main components:

A ___E:grapple fixture U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grapple_Fixture)___ was added to Zarya on STS-134 to enable Canadarm2 to inchworm itself onto the ROS. The critical systems are the atmosphere control system, the water supply system, the food supply facilities, the sanitation and hygiene equipment, and fire detection and suppression equipment.
The Russian Orbital Segment's life-support systems are contained in the Zvezda service module.
Some of these systems are supplemented by equipment in the USOS. The Nauka laboratory has a complete set of life-support systems.
The atmosphere on board the ISS is similar to ___E:that of Earth U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmosphere_of_Earth)___ .
Normal air pressure on the ISS is 101.3 kPa (14.69 psi);  the same as at sea level on Earth.

An Earth-like atmosphere offers benefits for crew comfort, and is much safer than a pure oxygen atmosphere, because of the increased risk of a fire such as that responsible for the deaths of the ___E:Apollo 1 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_1)___ crew.  [better source needed] Earth-like atmospheric conditions have been maintained on all Russian and Soviet spacecraft.
The Elektron system aboard Zvezda and a similar system in Destiny generate oxygen aboard the station.

The crew has a backup option in the form of bottled oxygen and ___E:Solid Fuel Oxygen Generation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vika_oxygen_generator)___ (SFOG) canisters, a ___E:chemical oxygen generator U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_oxygen_generator)___ system.
Carbon dioxide is removed from the air by the ___E:Vozdukh U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISS_ECLSS#Vozdukh)___ system in Zvezda .

Other by-products of human metabolism, such as methane from the intestines and ammonia from sweat, are removed by ___E:activated charcoal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Activated_carbon)___ filters.
Part of the ROS atmosphere control system is the oxygen supply.
Triple-redundancy is provided by the Elektron unit, solid fuel generators, and stored oxygen.

The 1 kW (1.3 hp) system uses approximately one litre of water per crew member per day. This water is either brought from Earth or recycled from other systems.

The secondary oxygen supply is provided by burning oxygen-producing ___E:Vika U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vika_oxygen_generator)___ cartridges (see also ___E:ISS ECLSS U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISS_ECLSS)___ ).

The US Orbital Segment (USOS) has redundant supplies of oxygen, from a pressurised storage tank on the Quest airlock module delivered in 2001, supplemented ten years later by ESA-built Advanced Closed-Loop System (ACLS) in the Tranquility module (Node 3), which produces O2 by electrolysis.
Hydrogen produced is combined with carbon dioxide from the cabin atmosphere and converted to water and methane.

Double-sided ___E:solar arrays U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_panel)___ provide ___E:electrical power U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_power)___ to the ISS. These bifacial cells collect direct sunlight on one side and light ___E:reflected off U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albedo)___ from the Earth on the other, and are more efficient and operate at a lower temperature than single-sided cells commonly used on Earth.

The Russian segment of the station, like most spacecraft, uses 28 ___E:V U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volt)___ ___E:low voltage U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extra-low_voltage)___ ___E:DC U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_current)___ from two rotating solar arrays mounted on Zvezda .
The USOS uses 130–180 V DC from the USOS PV array.

Power is stabilised and distributed at 160 V DC and converted to the user-required 124 V DC. The ___E:higher distribution voltage U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_voltage)___ allows smaller, lighter conductors, at the expense of crew safety.
The two station segments share power with converters.
The USOS solar arrays are arranged as four wing pairs, for a total production of 75 to 90 kilowatts.
These arrays normally track the Sun to maximise power generation.

Each array is about 375 m 2 (4,036 sq ft) in area and 58 m (190 ft) long. In the complete configuration, the solar arrays track the Sun by rotating the alpha gimbal once per orbit; the beta gimbal follows slower changes in the angle of the Sun to the orbital plane.

The ___E:Night Glider mode U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Night_Glider_mode)___ aligns the solar arrays parallel to the ground at night to reduce the significant aerodynamic drag at the station's relatively low orbital altitude.

The station originally used rechargeable ___E:nickel–hydrogen batteries U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nickel%E2%80%93hydrogen_battery)___ ( NiH2 ) for continuous power during the 45 minutes of every 90-minute orbit that it is eclipsed by the Earth.
The batteries are recharged on the day side of the orbit.
They had a 6.5-year lifetime (over 37,000 charge/discharge cycles) and were regularly replaced over the anticipated 20-year life of the station.

Starting in 2016, the nickel–hydrogen batteries were replaced by ___E:lithium-ion batteries U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithium-ion_battery)___ , which are expected to last until the end of the ISS program.
The station's large solar panels generate a high potential voltage difference between the station and the ionosphere.
This could cause arcing through insulating surfaces and sputtering of conductive surfaces as ions are accelerated by the spacecraft plasma sheath.
To mitigate this, ___E:plasma contactor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plasma_contactor)___ units create current paths between the station and the ambient space plasma.

The station's systems and experiments consume a large amount of electrical power, almost all of which is converted to heat. To keep the internal temperature within workable limits, a passive thermal control system (PTCS) is made of external surface materials, insulation such as MLI, and heat pipes.
If the PTCS cannot keep up with the heat load, an External Active Thermal Control System (EATCS) maintains the temperature.

The EATCS consists of an internal, non-toxic, water coolant loop used to cool and dehumidify the atmosphere, which transfers collected heat into an external liquid ___E:ammonia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ammonia)___ loop. From the heat exchangers, ammonia is pumped into external radiators that emit heat as infrared radiation, then the ammonia is cycled back to the station.
The EATCS provides cooling for all the US pressurised modules, including Kibō and Columbus , as well as the main power distribution electronics of the S0, S1 and P1 trusses.

It can reject up to 70 kW. This is much more than the 14 kW of the Early External Active Thermal Control System (EEATCS) via the Early Ammonia Servicer (EAS), which was launched on ___E:STS-105 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-105)___ and installed onto the P6 Truss.

The ISS relies on various radio communication systems to provide ___E:telemetry U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telemetry)___ and scientific data links between the station and ___E:mission control centres U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mission_control_center)___ .

Radio links are also used during ___E:rendezvous and docking procedures U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_rendezvous)___ and for audio and video communication between crew members, flight controllers and family members.
As a result, the ISS is equipped with internal and external communication systems used for different purposes.
The Russian Orbital Segment primarily uses the Lira antenna mounted on Zvezda for direct ground communication.

It also had the capability to utilize the Luch data relay satellite system,  which was in a state of disrepair when the station was built,    but was restored to operational status in 2011 and 2012 with the launch of Luch-5A and Luch-5B.
Additionally, the ___E:Voskhod-M U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voskhod-M)___ system provides internal telephone communications and VHF radio links to ground control.

The ___E:US Orbital Segment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Orbital_Segment)___ (USOS) makes use of two separate radio links: ___E:S band U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S_band)___ (audio, telemetry, commanding – located on the P1/S1 truss) and ___E:Ku band U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ku_band)___ (audio, video and data – located on the ___E:Z1 truss U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z1_truss)___ ) systems.

These transmissions are routed via the United States ___E:Tracking and Data Relay Satellite U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tracking_and_Data_Relay_Satellite)___ System (TDRSS) in ___E:geostationary orbit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geostationary_orbit)___ , allowing for almost continuous real-time communications with ___E:Christopher C. Kraft Jr. Mission Control Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_C._Kraft_Jr._Mission_Control_Center)___ (MCC-H) in ___E:Houston U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston)___ , Texas.

Data channels for the Canadarm2, European Columbus laboratory and Japanese Kibō modules were originally also routed via the S band and K u band systems, with the ___E:European Data Relay System U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Data_Relay_System)___ and a similar Japanese system intended to eventually complement the TDRSS in this role.
___E:UHF radio U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultra_high_frequency)___ is used by astronauts and cosmonauts conducting EVAs and other spacecraft that dock to or undock from the station.

Automated spacecraft are fitted with their own communications equipment; the ATV used a ___E:laser U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laser)___ attached to the spacecraft and the Proximity Communications Equipment attached to Zvezda to accurately dock with the station.
The US Orbital Segment of the ISS is equipped with approximately 100 ___E:commercial off-the-shelf U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_off-the-shelf)___ laptops running Windows or Linux.
These devices are modified to use the station's 28V DC power system and with additional ventilation since heat generated by the devices can stagnate in the weightless environment.
NASA prefers to keep a high commonality between laptops and spare parts are kept on the station so astronauts can repair laptops when needed.
The laptops are divided into two groups: the Portable Computer System (PCS) and Station Support Computers (SSC).

PCS laptops run Linux and are used for connecting to the station's primary Command & Control computer (C&C MDM), which runs on ___E:Debian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debian)___ Linux,  a switch made from Windows in 2013 for reliability and flexibility.

The primary computer supervises the critical systems that keep the station in orbit and supporting life.  Since the primary computer has no display or keyboards, astronauts use a PCS laptop to connect as remote terminals via a USB to ___E:1553 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MIL-STD-1553)___ adapter.
The primary computer experienced failures in 2001,  2007,  and 2017. The 2017 failure required a spacewalk to replace external components.

SSC laptops are used for everything else on the station, including reviewing procedures, managing scientific experiments, communicating over e-mail or video chat, and for entertainment during downtime.

SSC laptops connect to the station's ___E:wireless LAN U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wireless_LAN)___ via ___E:Wi-Fi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wi-Fi)___ , which connects to the ground via the K u band. While originally this provided speeds of 10 ___E:Mbit/s U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megabit_per_second)___ download and 3 Mbit/s upload from the station,  NASA upgraded the system in 2019 and increased the speeds to 600 Mbit/s.  ISS crew members have access to the ___E:internet U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet)___ .
Each permanent crew is given an expedition number.
Expeditions run up to six months, from launch until undocking, an 'increment' covers the same time period, but includes cargo spacecraft and all activities.
Expeditions 1 to 6 consisted of three-person crews.

After the destruction of NASA's Space Shuttle Columbia , Expeditions 7 to 12 were reduced to two-person "caretaker" crews who could maintain the station, because a larger crew could not be fully resupplied by the small Russian Progress cargo spacecraft.

After the Shuttle fleet returned to flight, three person crews also returned to the ISS beginning with Expedition 13. As the Shuttle flights expanded the station, crew sizes also expanded, eventually reaching six around 2010.   With the arrival of crew on larger US ___E:commercial spacecraft U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Development_of_the_Commercial_Crew_Program)___ beginning in 2020,  crew size has been increased to seven, the number for which ISS was originally designed.

There are currently eight docking ports for visiting spacecraft, with four additional ports installed but not yet put into service:

___E:Forward U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ship_directions)___ ports are at the front of the station in its usual orientation and direction of travel. ___E:Aft U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ship_directions)___ is the opposite, at the rear. ___E:Nadir U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadir)___ points toward Earth, while ___E:zenith U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zenith)___ points away from it. ___E:Port U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_and_starboard)___ is to the left and ___E:starboard U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_and_starboard)___ to the right when one's feet are toward Earth and one is facing forward, in the direction of travel.

Uncrewed spaceflights are primarily used to deliver cargo to the station including crew supplies, scientific investigations, spacewalk equipment, vehicle hardware, propellant, water, and gases.
Cargo resupply missions have typically used Russian Progress spacecraft, the now-retired European ATV, the Japanese HTV, and American Dragon and Cygnus spacecraft.
Additionally, several Russian modules have been launched on uncrewed rockets and autonomously docked with the station.
